newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks should lend more cheaply, says RBI.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks should lend more cheaply, says RBI.

text.p: Banks should strive to reduce the spread between the cost of raising funds and the rate at which they are lent, the Reserve Bank of India said on Wednesday.

"Banks must pass on the greater part of the efficiency gains to the borrowers in the form of lower lending rates," RBI said in its "Report on trend and progress of banking in India, 1995/96 (July-June)."
Banks would have to exercise their freedom to determine interest rates with caution as high lending rates could lead to a deterioration in their loans portfolio, the RBI warned.
"Too high a lending rate is not necessarily an advantage to banks," it said. "Very high lending rates may be associated with higher risks resulting in what the literature calls "adverse selection."
High rates could affect borrowers' capacity to repay, the RBI cautioned. They would be unsustainable as they might eventually result in an increase in the non-performing assets of banks, it said.

Commenting on banking developments and policy perspectives, the central bank said the first phase of banking sector reforms, part of India's overall economic reforms programme initiated in the early 1990s, was coming to an end.
The first phase of banking reforms concentrated on cleaning bank balance sheets and giving greater freedom to banks on determining individual interest rates.
The thrust of the second phase of reforms would be on improving the organisational efficiency of banks and other financial institutions, the RBI stated.
Banks should move away from excessive emphasis on asset management and adopt a more general approach of asset-liability management and management of credit risks, it said.
The RBI also called for an improvement in customer service.
